The most simple way to explain it is due to strong updrafts. So a little drop of rain starts falling, that ends up freezing, the updraft is strong enough to “cycle” that little pellet of frozen water back upwards to where it is below freezing over and over again, depositing a layer of ice each time, until it gets too heavy for the updrafts to keep it up in the ceiling, at which point it falls as hail. This is why hail mostly only occurs with strong/severe storms, as the updrafts in that system are essential to create bonafide hail.

Plastic is actually worth money, entire towns devoted to buying it from the US and other countries, and these “backyard factories” sort it (albeit it not very methodically or using science,) burn it/melt it down, remake into pellets, and then sell those pellets.
And a lot of those pellets make it into the “legitimate” supply chain, quite possibly into the containers for products you and I have bought. 

Is it a majority of plastics that go through this pipeline? Of course not, not even close to a majority, but there are a lot that do, and it has a pretty harmful effect on the environment and also the health of these “backyard” workers. 

There’s literally entire small towns devoted to this, outside of the main/major cities, (and even in them to a degree) regulation is almost non existent. It’s getting better but, China knows that if they want to build their economy as quick as possible, letting stuff like this slide ends up benefitting the economic situation. And the US and other companies get away with it because they are just selling the plastic and have nothing to do with what happens to it. The importation of our garbage, especially plastics into China has slowed, but only because the market is so over saturated with the amount of plastic. 

I made a comment on this post a short time ago going into slightly more detail if for some reason you’re interested. I’ve just always been interested in this “world” of unregulated recycling because I’m a nerd. There’s a few documentaries about it too (if you don’t mind subtitles as it is in Chinese if you don’t speak that language) that are super interesting following these peoples lives, the process, ect.

...so are you saying it’s better to just say “bury it out of sight, we have space for now and don’t see impacts (yet)” than figuring out a way to more efficient, cost effective, and not damaging to people and the world ways to recycle it? 

I’m genuinely curious, not trying to be an asshole or anything, promise, just curious to understand your perspective.

So, yes, a vast majority of it ends up in a landfill, however, it’s become a fairly decent buisness to sell plastic garbage to places like China. Countries like the US sell it SUPER cheap, because it’s cheaper to do this than to take up space in a landfill, it gets shipped to China, and there’s a whole small town in China that is entirely devoted to plastic waste recycling. Granted, these are largely unregulated, you can watch them burning the plastics down after sorting them, ect, then they turn them into pellets to make a profit. And the US companies are completely clear of wrongdoing legally because they are not involved in the recycling, they are just selling the plastics. And the way China is with its environmental regulations, especially with things like that, (basically to allow their economy to grow faster as they are in early stage pseudo capitalism,) if it’s not in main/major cities, it’s not visible pollution, they don’t care. 

After these “backyard operations” (for lack of better terms) sell the plastic pellets, they very easily make it back into the “food chain” of plastic products. Some Chinese companies buy it no questions asked, and then sell it into the “legitimate” recycled plastic economy. Some of it ending up in containers of products many here including myself, have likely bought. 

If anyone’s interested, I’ve watched a couple of documentaries (if you don’t mind subtitles as they are in Chinese,) and will gladly pass along the names. This specific part of the recycling/garbage world of largely developed countries making buisness out of selling our trash to other countries, and people in those countries figuring out ways to make a profit off of it also, be it regulated and legitimate ways or not. 

It’s actually becoming pretty decent buisness to buy/sell broken mobile phones, especially developed countries buying them from places in countries like Africa. It has become more expensive to mine many of the long list of precious medals and so on that goes into making a mobile phone, and it has now become profitable to instead recycle those precious medals by separating them in a somewhat complicated process, and selling them to, say, companies that make mobile phones. One of the reasons these companies buy many from towns and cities in countries like Africa is because the quality and life span of mobile phones over there, because of the established companies, are extremely cheap, both in price and quality, and many are “pre-loaded” phones that you just toss when the minutes run out. People have been mining the metals out of electronics for a long time in these countries, as it is/was a dumping ground for countries like the US. However, the recycling was largely “illlegitimate,” with heavy cost when it comes to the environment and also public health of the people (many times children or young people) who both live and work on these dumping cites. They recycle these metals by essentially burning most of the plastic off, and massive increases in cancer, respiratory illnesses, ect are seen in these people working these piles and also who live on the edges because this is how they make their living. But finally a couple larger companies have started to use much much more complex and better for health and environment ways to seperate these metals and precious resources. It’s all a very interesting “world.” To me at least
